content.title: What is the Thread Lifecycle?
content.description: The Thread Lifecycle describes the different states a thread passes through from its creation until its termination. Java defines these states using the Thread.State enum.

content.content: Every thread in Java moves through a series of well-defined states during its execution. Understanding these states helps developers write efficient multithreaded applications, debug concurrency issues, and optimize application performance.

content.title: Why Learn Thread Lifecycle?
content.content: Knowledge of thread states helps in debugging deadlocks, synchronization issues, waiting threads, and performance bottlenecks in concurrent applications.
Thread States in Java
The Thread.State enum defines six official thread states that represent the lifecycle of a thread.

rows: Thread object is created but not started.
Thread is ready to run and waiting for CPU scheduling.
Thread is waiting to acquire a monitor lock.
Thread waits indefinitely until another thread notifies it.
Thread waits for a specified amount of time.

content.title: Key Idea
content.description: A thread does not directly move from NEW to RUNNING. It first enters the RUNNABLE state and is scheduled by the JVM.

content.content: NEW State
A thread enters the NEW state immediately after its object is created. At this stage, the thread has not yet begun execution.

content.title: Creating a Thread
content.code:
Thread t = new Thread();
System.out.println(t.getState()); // NEW

content.content: RUNNABLE State
Calling start() moves the thread into the RUNNABLE state. The thread waits until the JVM scheduler assigns CPU time.

content.title: Starting a Thread
content.code:
Thread t = new Thread(() -> System.out.println("Running"));
t.start();

content.title: Important Note
content.content: RUNNABLE does not always mean the thread is executing. It simply means the thread is eligible to run.
BLOCKED State
A thread enters the BLOCKED state when it attempts to acquire a synchronized lock that is currently held by another thread.
WAITING State
A thread enters the WAITING state when it waits indefinitely for another thread to perform an action, such as calling notify() or notifyAll().
TIMED_WAITING State
A thread enters the TIMED_WAITING state when it waits for a specified duration using methods such as sleep(), join(timeout), or wait(timeout).
TERMINATED State
Once the run() method completes or an uncaught exception occurs, the thread enters the TERMINATED state and cannot be restarted.

content.content: Real-Life Analogy

content.title: Customer at a Bank
content.content: A customer first enters the bank (NEW), waits in the queue (RUNNABLE), gets served (Running), may wait for document verification (WAITING/BLOCKED), and finally leaves the bank (TERMINATED).

content.title: Interview Importance
content.content: Interviewers frequently ask about Thread.State values, Runnable vs Running, sleep(), wait(), notify(), join(), synchronization, deadlocks, and state transitions.
Common Mistakes

items.question: Can a terminated thread be restarted?
items.answer: No. Once terminated, a thread cannot be started again.

items.question: Is RUNNABLE the same as Running?
items.answer: No. RUNNABLE means eligible to run, while Running means the CPU is actively executing the thread.

items.question: Does sleep() release synchronization locks?
items.answer: No. A sleeping thread retains any locks it currently owns.

content.title: Remember This
content.description: A thread progresses through NEW, RUNNABLE, WAITING/BLOCKED/TIMED_WAITING (if needed), and TERMINATED. The JVM scheduler controls execution after start() is called.

content.title: Quick Revision
points: start() moves a thread to RUNNABLE.
WAITING and TIMED_WAITING differ in timeout behavior.
BLOCKED occurs while waiting for a lock.
TERMINATED is the final state and cannot be reversed.
